rationale: The full review discusses urinary urgency with white-matter lesions and extra-virgin olive oil separately in a vascular microparticle context. It supplies no oil and urinary comparison in Parkinson disease.

Review names black tea extract rat motor study Chaturvedi 2006 and theaflavin animal models; these are previously catalogued original studies, not an independent brewed-tea clinical bradykinesia comparison.
Table cites Chaturvedi 2006 oral black-tea extract in 6-OHDA rats and spontaneous locomotion and amphetamine-induced circling; it does not establish a brewed-tea clinical bradykinesia score.
The tannin review names black tea as a dietary source of proanthocyanidins and bradykinesia as a Parkinson symptom, not a measured brewed-tea symptom comparison.
The alpha-synuclein review describes bradykinesia clinically and cites black tea among possible disease-risk factors, without a measured tea-treated bradykinesia outcome.
The alpha-synuclein review cites isolated black-tea theaflavins for in-vitro protein aggregation, separate from the clinical bradykinesia background; no brewed tea motor comparison.
Physical-activity review discusses incident Parkinson associations for black tea and separate exercise treatment outcomes; incidence is not a tea effect on established bradykinesia.
Section 6.10 summarizes isolated theaflavin animal motor studies, not brewed tea or measured clinical bradykinesia; a related 2012 subacute report was retracted and must not be credited.
The mitochondrial review cites tea polyphenol radical scavenging and dopamine-neuron mechanisms; no brewed-black-tea bradykinesia comparison is reported.
Bibliometric review cites isolated theaflavin and black-tea extract studies; its separate table entry linking rat bradykinesia to Kim 2010 refers to mulberry fruit, not black tea.
The prodromal-risk review discusses caffeine-containing beverages including black tea and incident Parkinson disease; this is not a bradykinesia treatment result.
Review cites tea consumption in disease risk and possible progression and lists bradykinesia as a feature; no item-level brewed-black-tea clinical comparison is reported.
The cognition symposium cites foods associated with cognition in non-Parkinson samples. Its clinical anxiety discussion concerns evaluating cognition and gives no chocolate intervention.

The cocoa section links general mood and cocoa constituents to other studies. The Parkinson chocolate study concerns consumption and depression screening, and the crossover assesses motor findings. Neither reports a dark-chocolate anxiety estimate.
The antioxidant review mentions dark chocolate in a microbiota discussion. Anxiety examples concern neurotransmitters or other interventions, without a chocolate and anxiety comparison.
The rotenone rat study has a 95% cacao chocolate arm given as powder dispersed in water. The prespecified readouts are microbiota, biochemical and tissue measures, with no scored anxiety behavior.
The review mentions cocoa flavonoids in broad dietary strategies. Its separate anxiety and neurotransmitter discussion gives no measured chocolate and clinical anxiety comparison.
Rosemary is listed among suggested anti-inflammatory foods for rheumatoid arthritis, not an observed fresh rosemary intervention or PD depression outcome.
Rosemary is cited as a source of isolated linalool or borneol and reviewed preclinical neuroprotection; no fresh rosemary PD depression comparison.

Publisher subscription preview reviews isolated rosmarinic acid across nervous system disorders including PD and depression. Full body unavailable; no fresh rosemary clinical comparison is established from abstract.
Rosemary discussion covers essential oils, compounds and preclinical neural models, not fresh culinary rosemary for depression in people with PD.
Rosemary Maguire is a Parkinson specialist nurse; the name is not a herbal exposure.
Review discusses rosemary or its constituents for enzyme inhibition and AD, while depression is a symptom context; no fresh rosemary PD depression comparison.
Rosemary is a food source of luteolin in zebrafish flavonoid review; isolated compound/model outcomes are not fresh rosemary PD depression.
Rosemary essential-oil nanoemulsion is applied topically in a mouse skin-aging model, not fresh dietary rosemary or depression.
Rosemary extract increases glucose uptake in neuronal cell lines, not fresh herb in people with PD or a depression outcome.
Rosemary listed as source of luteolin, an isolated flavone; no fresh rosemary PD depression outcome.
Rosemary is listed as source of luteolin in a review of isolated flavonoids and models; no fresh herb PD depression study.
Rosemary leaf is cataloged as traditionally good for nerves/stimulant; no measured fresh leaf depression comparison in PD.
PD brain-fog review discusses isolated carnosic acid from rosemary as a preclinical candidate without a clinical study; no fresh rosemary depression result.

Rosemary review describes depression trials in non-PD people using inhaled essential oil or distinct extracts and isolated compounds; no fresh culinary rosemary in PD. Table ambiguously labels rosmarinic acid essential oil; follow original references.
Dementia review discusses lemon balm essential oil, combination with valerian and historical melancholy use, not brewed lemon balm for PD depression.
Melissa is a trial investigator name; breast cancer depression trial uses melatonin, not lemon balm.
Melissa is a personal name in DLB consensus; no lemon balm intervention.
Melissa officinalis is a listed source of isolated linalool in preclinical models, not brewed lemon balm or a PD depression outcome.
Melissa Vos is an author of the Drosophila PD review, not a lemon balm exposure.
Melissa Armstrong is an author of the cognitive-impairment PD review, not a lemon balm exposure.
Cardioprotection review lists traditional depression use and extracts or isolated compounds; no brewed lemon balm PD depression comparison.
Insomnia review cites lemon balm extract for anxiety and sleep rather than brewed lemon balm for PD depressive symptoms.
Review describes hypothesized anxiolytic/antidepressant mechanisms and cites post-sepsis rat extract; no brewed lemon balm PD depression outcome.
Melissa German-Montenegro is an author of gut microbiota PD review, not a lemon balm intervention.
Melissa Sheth is an author of the PD synuclein review, not a lemon balm intervention.
Melissa occurs as personal name in depression genetics consortium; no lemon balm consumption comparison.
Aqueous Melissa extract is reviewed for manganese-induced oxidative stress in mice, not brewed tea or depression severity in PD.
Review discusses lemon balm aromatherapy for dementia agitation and aqueous extract in manganese-exposed mice; neither is brewed tea for PD depression.
Melissa is an author name in an fMRI dyslexia review, not lemon balm exposure.
Lemon balm leaves are listed as sedative in traditional plant table, without measured brewed tea PD depression comparison.
